subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Evolution and Adaptation
subtitle: Natural selection, inherited variation, adaptations, extinction, and evidence for evolution.
description: A source-faithful middle school life science revision pack on evolution and adaptation. Students review inherited variation, natural selection, adaptations, extinction, fossil and DNA evidence, real case studies, data interpretation, and common misconceptions.

data.targetWord: change in inherited traits of a population over many generations

examples.en-US: Evolution occurs when inherited traits become more or less common in a population over generations.

data.targetWord: an inherited trait that helps an organism survive or reproduce in a particular environment

examples.en-US: A cactus has waxy skin and spines that help it conserve water.

data.targetWord: a process where organisms with helpful inherited traits survive and reproduce more often

examples.en-US: Natural selection can make camouflaged moths more common when predators eat visible moths.

data.targetWord: differences in traits among individuals in a population

examples.en-US: Variation means some insects may be lighter or darker than others.

data.targetWord: a characteristic of an organism

examples.en-US: Fur color, beak shape, and leaf shape are traits.

data.targetWord: a trait passed from parents to offspring through genes

examples.en-US: A bird can inherit beak shape from its parents.

data.targetWord: a trait gained during life that is usually not passed through genes

examples.en-US: A scar is an acquired trait rather than an inherited trait.

data.targetWord: a group of organisms of the same species living in the same area

examples.en-US: All the deer in one forest form a population.

data.targetWord: a group of similar organisms that can usually reproduce with each other

examples.en-US: Gray wolves are one example of a species.

data.targetWord: all the living and nonliving things around an organism

examples.en-US: Food, water, predators, temperature, and sunlight are parts of an environment.

data.targetWord: success at surviving and reproducing in a specific environment

examples.en-US: A beetle that survives and leaves many offspring has high fitness in that environment.

data.targetWord: the process of making offspring

examples.en-US: Reproduction passes inherited traits to the next generation.

data.targetWord: new organisms produced by parents

examples.en-US: Seedlings and chicks are examples of offspring.

data.targetWord: one step in a family line from parents to offspring

examples.en-US: Parent mice and their baby mice are different generations.

data.targetWord: a change in DNA that can create new variation

examples.en-US: A mutation may change fur color or have no visible effect.

data.targetWord: a section of DNA that influences a trait

examples.en-US: A gene may affect flower color or blood type.

data.targetWord: the molecule that carries genetic instructions in cells

examples.en-US: Scientists compare DNA to study how closely species are related.

data.targetWord: preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms

examples.en-US: Bones, footprints, shells, and leaf prints can be fossils.

data.targetWord: all the fossils scientists have found and studied

examples.en-US: The fossil record helps scientists compare organisms from different times.

data.targetWord: the death of all members of a species

examples.en-US: Non-bird dinosaurs became extinct about 66 million years ago.

data.targetWord: an earlier species from which two or more later species evolved

examples.en-US: Wolves and coyotes share common ancestors.

data.targetWord: an environmental factor that affects survival or reproduction

examples.en-US: Predators, disease, drought, and competition can be selective pressures.

data.targetWord: a trait that helps an organism blend in with its surroundings

examples.en-US: A stick insect looks like a twig because of camouflage.

data.targetWord: a trait where one organism resembles another organism or object

examples.en-US: A harmless fly may resemble a stinging wasp.

data.targetWord: a struggle between organisms for limited resources

examples.en-US: Plants may compete for sunlight, water, and space.

data.targetWord: the variety of living things in an area

examples.en-US: A forest with many plants, insects, fungi, and animals has high biodiversity.

data.targetWord: human selection of organisms with desired traits for breeding

examples.en-US: People breed dogs for size, behavior, coat type, or working ability.

data.targetWord: a testable explanation or prediction

examples.en-US: A hypothesis can predict that dark beetles survive more often on dark bark.

data.targetWord: a factor that can change in an investigation

examples.en-US: Background color is a variable in a camouflage investigation.

data.targetWord: data or observations that support a scientific explanation

examples.en-US: A graph showing more dark beetles surviving on dark bark is evidence.

data.targetWord: a group of connected parts that interact

examples.en-US: A forest ecosystem is a system with organisms, soil, water, and sunlight.

data.targetWord: the ability to cause change or do work

examples.en-US: Organisms use energy from food to grow and reproduce.

data.targetWord: anything that has mass and takes up space

examples.en-US: Organisms are made of matter, and matter cycles through ecosystems.

data.targetWord: the study of similarities and differences in body structures across species

examples.en-US: Similar front limb bones in bats, whales, cats, and humans can suggest common ancestry.

data.targetWord: the study of early development in organisms

examples.en-US: Similar early embryos can provide clues about shared ancestry.

data.targetWord: evidence collected by watching changes happen in real time

examples.en-US: Scientists can directly observe evolution in bacteria and insects with short generation times.

data.targetWord: the ability of some bacteria to survive exposure to an antibiotic

examples.en-US: Resistant bacteria may survive antibiotic exposure and reproduce.

data.targetWord: a case study where moth color frequencies changed as tree bark color changed

examples.en-US: Dark peppered moths had an advantage on soot-darkened tree trunks.

data.targetWord: Galapagos birds whose beak shapes show how food availability can affect selection

examples.en-US: During droughts, finches with deeper beaks may survive better when hard seeds are common.

data.targetWord: a case study showing that fur color can be helpful or harmful depending on background color

examples.en-US: Dark fur helps mice blend in on lava but may stand out on pale sand.

data.targetWord: a situation where seasonal coat color no longer matches the background

examples.en-US: A white hare may be easier to see when winter ground has little snow.

data.targetWord: a scientific explanation format that links an answer, supporting data, and scientific ideas

examples.en-US: A CER response explains which beetle color had an advantage and why the data supports it.

data.title: Natural Selection Process
data.instruction: Put the main steps of natural selection in order.
items: Variation exists in a population.
More offspring are produced than can survive.
A selective pressure affects survival and reproduction.
Individuals with helpful inherited traits reproduce more successfully.
Helpful inherited traits become more common over generations.
The population evolves.

data.title: Antibiotic Resistance Over Generations
data.instruction: Order the events that can make antibiotic resistance more common.
items: A bacterial population contains some resistant bacteria.
An antibiotic kills many bacteria that are not resistant.
Resistant bacteria survive exposure more often.
Surviving resistant bacteria reproduce quickly.
Later generations contain a higher percentage of resistant bacteria.

data.title: Using Claim-Evidence-Reasoning
data.instruction: Put the parts of a strong scientific explanation in order.
items: Read the question and decide what claim answers it.
Choose data or observations that support the claim.
Explain the scientific idea that connects the evidence to the claim.
Check that the explanation refers to inherited traits, selection, and generations when needed.

data.title: Fossil Layer Reasoning
data.instruction: Order the reasoning scientists use with undisturbed rock layers.
items: Identify the rock layers and fossils in each layer.
Use relative position to infer that lower layers are usually older.
Compare fossils from older and younger layers.
Look for similarities and differences among related organisms.
Combine fossil evidence with other evidence such as DNA and anatomy.
